environmental-control-intro.title: Understanding Occupational Health and Environmental Control
environmental-control-intro.content: OSHA 1910 Subpart G addresses workplace hazards that are not always immediately visible. Dust, fumes, vapors, excessive noise, and radiation can cause lasting harm before symptoms appear. Engineering controls — such as ventilation systems, enclosures, and dust collectors — are the preferred first line of defense. PPE is important but should not be the only protection when hazards can be controlled at the source.

abrasive-blasting-ventilation.title: Ventilation for Abrasive Blasting Operations
abrasive-blasting-ventilation.content: Abrasive blasting creates respirable dust from both the abrasive material and the surface coating being removed. Blast-cleaning enclosures must maintain inward airflow at all openings. After blasting stops, the exhaust system must continue operating until all dusty air is cleared before any enclosure door is opened. Dust collectors must be maintained and respirators may be required depending on the operation.

grinding-polishing-ventilation.title: Ventilation for Grinding, Polishing, and Buffing
grinding-polishing-ventilation.content: Dry grinding, polishing, and buffing can produce dust, fumes, and gases that endanger workers. Exhaust hoods must be positioned so that contaminants are pulled away from the worker's breathing zone, not blown toward them. Hoods should be located as close as practical to the work source. Exhaust systems must include suitable dust collectors and be regularly maintained.

spray-finishing-ventilation.title: Spray Finishing Ventilation and Fire Safety
spray-finishing-ventilation.content: Spray finishing operations must be conducted inside spray booths or spray rooms built from noncombustible materials. Ventilation must control both overspray and solvent vapors. Make-up air must replace all air exhausted from the booth to maintain proper airflow. Filters, pressure gauges, doors, dampers, and louvers must be inspected and maintained. Ignition sources must be eliminated to prevent fire and explosion.

noise-exposure-hearing-conservation.title: Occupational Noise Exposure and Hearing Conservation
noise-exposure-hearing-conservation.content: OSHA 1910.95 requires a hearing conservation program when employees are exposed to noise at or above 85 dBA as an 8-hour time-weighted average. Employers must conduct noise monitoring to identify affected employees, notify them of results, and provide hearing protectors at no cost. Annual training in the hearing conservation program is required for all covered employees.

audiometric-testing-hearing-protection.title: Audiometric Testing, Hearing Protectors, and Follow-Up
audiometric-testing-hearing-protection.content: A baseline audiogram provides a reference for comparing future annual audiograms. When a standard threshold shift is detected, the employer must notify the employee in writing. Hearing protectors must be properly fitted and evaluated to ensure adequate attenuation for the specific noise environment. Noise exposure records and audiometric test records must be maintained according to OSHA requirements.

nonionizing-radiation-awareness.title: Nonionizing Radiation Awareness
nonionizing-radiation-awareness.content: OSHA 1910.97 covers radio-frequency and microwave radiation hazards from sources such as radar equipment, radio transmitters, navigation systems, and industrial RF equipment. Warning signs must identify radio-frequency radiation hazard areas. Employees must not enter restricted areas unless authorized and trained. Partial body exposure can still be hazardous, particularly to the eyes and other sensitive tissues.
